items.title: Every Wahoo Bike Computer Is Up to 35% Off for Black Friday—Here’s Which One to Buy
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: From the wind-sensing Ace to the compact Bolt 3, all three Elemnt units are on sale right now. Here is how they stack up and which one is best for you.
items.lbText:

Welcome to Velo Deals. We sift through the retail landscape to bring you deals worth paying attention to. It might be a discount or it might just be a product so good you should grab it. Either way, if it’s worth your time, you’ll see it here. If you’d like to see the rest of the category, check all our Velo Deals coverage.

When it comes to bike computers, the biggest players are Garmin and Wahoo, and each takes a fundamentally different approach to solving the same puzzle. If you want simple, Wahoo is the one for you, and all three size options are being offered at a massive discount right now.

Across the entire lineup, Wahoo makes the easiest-to-use bike computers on the market. They are the ultimate “it just works” devices: add your accounts, connect to Wi-Fi, and you’re ready to ride. You aren’t giving up serious metrics for that simplicity, either. Instead of painstakingly assigning data to individual boxes, you just list your fields in order of importance in the app and use the side buttons to zoom in or out on the fly. Even if you normally like a lot of data, it’s great to zoom in to just power and speed when it’s late in a ride, everything hurts, and you just need to pedal.

The main trade-off in the past was always that Wahoo doesn’t offer an all-encompassing 24/7 wearable ecosystem, but even that’s been fixed recently. Wahoo has a partnership with Coros, and if you want a full picture of both training and recovery, you can use the Coros backend system and a Coros watch seamlessly with your Wahoo computer.

At the top of the lineup sits the Elemnt Ace, which is Wahoo’s answer for riders who want maximum screen real estate and every feature the brand makes. It has a large 3.8-inch color touchscreen, 64GB of storage, dual-band GPS, a built-in speaker for voice turn-by-turn navigation, and up to 30 hours of claimed battery life. Its headline differentiator is an integrated wind sensor that measures live airspeed to quantify headwinds, tailwinds, and drafting. All of that hardware comes with a clear trade-off in size and weight—at 208 grams, it is noticeably larger and heavier than a standard head unit, which is why Wahoo includes an aluminum out-front mount in the box.

This is probably the one you really want. It keeps almost everything that makes the Ace appealing—including the 16-million-color touchscreen interface, 64GB of storage, dual-band GPS, and the built-in speaker for audible turn-by-turn prompts—while dropping the wind sensor and massive size. Instead of a 3.8-inch display, it steps down to a still very usable 2.8-inch screen and cuts the weight nearly in half to 109 grams, with a claimed battery life of up to 25 hours.

If you want something smaller and lighter for racing or just prefer a cleaner cockpit, the Elemnt Bolt 3 strips the formula down to the essentials. This is also the best budget play, but it’s still a very capable computer. Weighing in at 84 grams with a 2.3-inch color display, it drops both the touchscreen and the audio speaker, relying strictly on physical buttons for control. Storage drops to 32GB and claimed battery life dips to 20 hours, but you still get the same dual-band GPS, high-contrast color screen tech, and updated Ready-To-Ride interface found on its bigger siblings.

items.title: These E-Bikes Make City Riding a Joy
items.author: Alison Jaksen
items.content: With lightweight, minimalist design, Aventon’s new rides turn urban streets into your personal playground
items.lbText:
The Aventon Solterra 3. (Photo: Aventon)

Riding a bike, at its heart, is amazing because it’s so simple. Two wheels, a frame, and suddenly you’re zooming around and discovering that going places can be fun . That’s why fixed-gear and single-speed bikes have such passionate fans: They prioritize the freedom that comes from embracing simplicity. With less weight and extraneous features, biking reenters the realm of play, and a daily commute or jaunt to grab groceries can feel a lot like flying.

Enter Aventon’s Soltera 2.5 and Soltera 3 ADV, which capture that fixie magic. The brand launched its legendary fixed gear Mataró model back in 2013, and that minimalist spirit infuses this new pair of e-bikes. They both marry a light-is-right sensibility with powerful but barely-there motors, all of it in a stealth design that will change the way you think about e-bikes.

The Class 1 Soltera 3 ADV Ebike ($1,499) will delight purists. Powered by a 250-watt (500-watt peak) motor, it offers 40 Nm of torque and a 70-mile range in a featherweight 37-pound package. It swaps a clanky chain for a carbon reinforced polymer belt that’s way easier to maintain and can last two to three times longer than any chain. Its single-speed configuration keeps you nimble and agile in the stop-start flow and narrow corridors you’ll encounter in urban traffic.

The Soltera 3’s updated geometry sings in the concrete maze, too—and everywhere. A longer wheelbase and lower bottom bracket keep it planted and predictable at speed, while a taller stack puts you in a more upright position that’s easier on your back, wrists, and neck on longer rides. A lower standover makes it easy to hop on and off at every light. With its ease of use and maintenance, there’s no simpler way to get some electric oomph into your daily ride.

Want to go down the zen road of simplicity but retain a bit more flex and options? You want the Soltera 2.5 Ebike ($1,199). For a scant 9 more pounds, you get a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain, on-demand throttle, wired features, and a 46-mile range. It brings a more traditional city e-bike feel while paring away the fluff to maintain fixie-forward geometry and feel.

Swapping your trusty-rusty analog commuting horse for an e-bike can feel like settling for an underpowered motorcycle. But both Soltera models deliver electric power while reaching back to a style of riding with less weight, complication, and stress—and more of what you need to make city streets fun to ride.

Aventon Bikes is here to inspire adventures, both big and small, in all terrains of life. No matter what we look like now, a year from now, or a decade from now, this is what keeps us moving forward. Redefine adventure and learn more at aventon.com .

items.title: One Editor Thinks 32-Inch Gravel Is the Future. Another Gives It Five Years.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Logan makes the case for bigger wheels, Mike blames bad geometry, Lisa sees a Big Wheel, and Blue Hat Guy puts a five-year expiration date on the whole standard.
items.lbText:
The Velo Podcast wouldn’t happen without subscribers. We’re offering listeners of the show a special 25% discount on an Outside+ membership. Enter the code velopod at checkout to score these savings, and thank you for your support!

This week, the full crew is together to do some arguing. Host Mike Levy, Lisa Charlebois, Logan Jones-Wilkins, and I (Josh Ross, though Blue Hat Guy works too) are debating Zwift versus everyone and whether 32-inch wheels are actually here to stay.

Before we get to the main event, we dive into a pile of listener comments from last week’s indoor riding and Zwift Plus discussion. That includes everything from TrainerRoad or Strava versus Zwift (and why fearing for life on rollers might be the best way) to whether Zwift will eventually fold Rouvy into a single platform. For the record, I’m putting my prediction on the board now: Rouvy ceases to exist as a separate thing in three years. We also tackle a listener theory that virtual cars in Zwift video routes are desensitizing indoor-first riders to real traffic—a take that leaves Mike and me pretty much speechless before Logan steps in with a much more reasonable explanation.

From there, it is time for the topic everyone loves to hate: 32-inch gravel wheels. Logan just wrapped up 500 miles on the MMosaic GT i55 32—a custom titanium bike built around a proper 32-inch carbon fork—and he is a huge fan. He argues it makes gravel riding noticeably more fun, with better rollover, more traction, and geometry that actually makes sense off-road. Mike agrees, arguing that the best thing about 32-inch wheels isn’t even the wheels themselves, but the longer, more stable geometry they force frame builders to adopt.

I am on the other side of the fence. While I don’t doubt the off-road performance gains exist, my argument is a business one: consumers have wheel-size fatigue, brands don’t want to manage multiple standards, and 32-inch gravel bikes are headed for the same fate as 650b within five years. That leads to a back-and-forth over whether brands can actually pull off two wheel sizes across a single frame run (when they still struggle to spec the right handlebar widths), whether 700c gravel bikes are just turning into “all-road” bikes, and what all of this means for shorter riders who don’t want to feel like they’re riding a monster truck.

Lisa: “This is gonna sound so dumb. I’m sorry, everybody. But it looks like you’re on a Big Wheel… It just looks so weird. The scale is so wrong.” Mike: “We all look so weird. We’re wearing spandex riding bicycles around, talking about watts and carbs. We look stupid and I love it.” Logan: “You know how many people noticed I was riding 32 at Big Sugar? Zero people. Nobody noticed.” Lisa: “Yeah, but you’re tall, dude. You look in proportion.”

As always, let us know where you land in the comments—are you with Logan on the 32-inch future, or are you siding with Blue Hat Guy? And make sure to vote in this week’s poll below to tell us whether you’re actually planning to buy a 32-inch gravel bike when they hit the market in force.

items.title: Stinner Frameworks Launches Stoic Components With Three New Wheelsets
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The Santa Barbara-based bike builder launched the wheels under the new sub-brand, as well as a few other upgrades.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Stinner Frameworks has a lot more wheels to build with. The metal frame builder based in Santa Barbara has launched Stoic Components, a sub-brand within the company, to manufacture carbon wheels built to match the bikes in Stinner’s catalog.

The component brand is a long time in the making for Stinner. In the press release, Stinner said the brand has been in the making for a decade, stemming from a collaboration with Jones Wheel’s late founder John Jones.

“John and I planned to start a component brand together,” Aaron Stinner, the founder of Stinner Frameworks, said. We lost him to cancer in 2021, before we got the chance. Stoic Components is that brand. We’re starting where he would have: carbon wheels, each matched to a Stinner frame and laced to Stoic hubs.”

Each wheelset will start at $1,499 and use the same basic ingredients: Pillar PSR Triple Butted J-bend spokes, Toray T700/T800 carbon, and in-house hubs. The wheels also have a 265-pound rider weight limit, sealed cartridge bearings, and specific asymmetric rim profiles.

Beyond the new wheels, Stinner has also unveiled a collection of other updates. The Stinner Select range of bikes now uses higher-quality Columbus Life tubing and improved specs. Stinner Select 2.0 framesets will now cost $2,599, while complete builds start at $5,499.

Additionally, if you have wondered how I capture my bike imagery, I have been a long-time user of Stinner’s Photo Stick. The small titanium tool is built to easily prop a bike up for photos while packing down small enough to fit in a carry-on bag or a rear pocket. It uses a three-point construction to provide a strong lean point to prop the bike up wherever seems fit.

Stinner has released a new Photo Stick 2.0, also called the Photostique, which is available now for $109.99 MSRP.

To learn more about the Stoic Component wheels or the brand’s other upgrades, check out Stinner’s website .

items.title: Tadej Pogačar Hints at Monster 2027 After His Brutal Vuelta Crash
items.author: ahood
items.content: Flanders and Roubaix again? Tadej Pogačar drops some fresh clues on his calendar and weighs in on what the Tour de France route means for 2027.
items.lbText:
Pogačar hinted that Flanders and Roubaix could be in the cards for 2027. (Photo: Gruber Images)

If anyone is doubting Tadej Pogačar and what his brutal crash at the Vuelta a España might mean for 2027, rest assured.

Don’t worry, Pogi fans, it doesn’t appear that anything will change.

Pogačar sounds as ambitious as ever and said a return to the Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix could be in the cards in 2027.

“There is a good chance that I will be at the start again, yes,” he told HLN . “I am already looking forward to it, because they are fun races.”

“Fun” for Pogačar usually means misery for everyone else, but fans absolutely love seeing the world No. 1 race the iconic northern classics .

Pogačar has already singled out the Tour de France , unfinished business at the Vuelta, and a run at a record-tying third worlds in Sallanches as major goals for 2027.

Some wondered if that loaded back-end calendar might mean an easier start to next season, especially since he hasn’t raced since his crash on August 29.

But from what Pogačar told the Belgian outlet Het Laatste Nieuws at the annual padel tournament hosted by his agent Alex Carera in Italy, it doesn’t sound like it.

The quick grab with journalists provided some fresh hints of what next year’s comeback season might look like.

Pogačar admitted the obvious that the 71km of time trial kilometers in the 2027 Tour suits Remco Evenepoel. He also made it clear that he still sees Jonas Vingegaard as a contender on any course.

King Pog doesn’t appear to be losing any sleep over it either, even if some are hyping the 2027 Tour as the “Anti-Pogačar” course .

“I haven’t really looked at the course in detail yet, but there is indeed some time trialing involved,” he said. “That is good for Remco, but as I always say, in the Tour, you can’t hide anywhere. You have to be strong for three weeks in every discipline.

“Whether that’s uphill or on the time trial bike. And you have to be able to maintain focus. That won’t be any different next year.”

The Tour is all but certain to be at the center of his calendar for 2027. After winning the record-tying fifth yellow jersey, he wants to make official history by going for number six.

If he does show up for the Flanders-Roubaix double again, that’s the best indication yet there won’t be any lingering physical impacts from the Vuelta crash.

Roubaix and the Vuelta remain one of the few major races Pogačar has yet to win .

After a few weeks off the bike following surgery in September, Pogačar is back to training after the heavy crash that ended his Vuelta and cut short his 2026 season.

After missing the worlds in Montréal, his UAE teammate Brandon McNulty will be racing in the rainbow jersey , so this season Pogačar won’t be donning the stripes.

“I enjoyed the off-season. The first training sessions didn’t go very smoothly, but things have been going better for the past week,” he said. “My rides are getting longer and I can already pick up the intensity a bit.”

Pogačar’s social media feed has been filled with weddings, trips, coffee rides, sessions in the gym, some jogging, lots of food, and yes, a few longer bike rides.

After two documentaries recently dropped , Pocačar is enjoying his last few days of quiet home life before joining his UAE Emirates-XRG teammates in Spain next month for the team’s first winter camp.

That’s when Pogačar’s official racing calendar will be sketched out.

We’ll see what team boss Mauro Gianetti has to say.

He tapped the brakes on Pogačar’s desire to return to racing for the European championships in Slovenia, and it was a good thing too, because doctors later found other neck fractures from his Vuelta spill .

From the sounds of things, if Pogačar has his way, he won’t be slowing down at all in 2027.

items.title: Mario Cipollini Stalking and Abuse Case Ends as Statute of Limitations Expires
items.author: ahood
items.content: An Italian court ended a stalking and abuse case against former world champion Mario Cipollini and vacated his three-year sentence after the statute of limitations expired.
items.lbText:
Criminal case against Mario Cipollini has ended in Italy. (Photo: Tim de Waele/Corbis via Getty Images)

An appeals court in Florence ended the criminal case against former road world champion Mario Cipollini on Thursday after ruling that the statute of limitations had expired on all counts.

Cipollini, 59, was facing a three-year prison term handed down by a Lucca court in 2022, Italian media reported .

The case began in 2017 when Cipollini’s ex-wife Sabrina Landucci filed a complaint. The charges included alleged domestic mistreatment, stalking, bodily harm, and threats.

Landucci reached a separate agreement with Cipollini over damages and withdrew from the proceedings, La Stampa reported.

“Today I can declare, without any fear of contradiction, that I am a citizen with a completely clean criminal record,” Cipollini wrote on Facebook.

He said his lawyers had challenged the Lucca court’s account of events, and that basically time had run out before an appeals court could hear a possible challenge.

Cipollini — nicknamed Il Re Leone (The Lion King) and Super Mario — retired in 2008 after a 20-year pro career. The flamboyant sprinter won the 2002 world title, 160 pro wins, Milan-San Remo , and a record 42 stage victories at the Giro d’Italia.

Cipollini often ran afoul with race organizers and the UCI for his outrageous antics, that included dressing up in a toga ahead of a stage at the Tour de France or racing in a zebra-print skin suit.

In 2008, he was linked to the Operación Puerto doping scandal, an allegation he denied. In 2013, the French Senate released a report that linked Cipollini as one of the riders whose samples from the 1998 Tour de France were positive for traces of EPO when retested in 2004.

Since retiring, Cipollini has remained in the public eye, with appearances on Italy’s version of “Dancing With The Stars” and other reality TV programs.

Cipollini launched his own bike brand in 2010 and November 2025 he underwent heart surgery in Ancona, Italian media reported last year.

items.title: George Hincapie’s Son and Another Rising American Teen Are in Red Bull’s WorldTour Pipeline. How Far Can They Go?
items.author: ahood
items.content: Enzo Hincapie moves up to Red Bull’s U23 Rookies and Jack Klau joins the junior team. Could the American teens one day race with Remco Evenepoel?
items.lbText:
Enzo Hincapie gets promoted to Red Bull's U23 squad in 2027. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

Two of America’s most promising teens — Enzo Hincapie and Jack Klau — are moving up in the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe talent pipeline in 2027.

Hincapie, 18, steps up to the U23 Red Bull Rookies after winning the U.S. junior national title.

Klau, 17, signs with the U19 junior team grenke-Auto Eder.

That puts two Americans right in the center of Red Bull’s development train that runs directly from the junior team to the Rookies and on to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe WorldTour squad.

This is cycling’s version of getting drafted out of high school by the Yankees. Red Bull has one of the peloton’s biggest budgets and is betting big on development, but the odds are still long of hitting the WorldTour.

Could these two up end up as Remco Evenepoel’s teammate in a few years?

Red Bull rolled out its rosters for its two development squads for 2027, and the two Americans both get star billing.

Hincapie — the son of former pro George Hincapie — spent 2026 on Red Bull’s grenke-Auto Eder U19 squad. Standout rides include victory at the U.S. junior title and fourth at the junior Tour of Flanders.

Those results helped earn him one of four promotions from the junior squad to the Rookies for 2027.

That bump is significant because Red Bull is investing heavily on its development programs to build out its WorldTour team.

Four Red Bull Rookies from the U23 squad — Tour de l’Avenir winner Lorenzo Finn , Alessio Magagnotti, Davide Donati and Sebastian Putz — are graduating to Red Bull’s WorldTour lineup in 2027.

“In 2026 we had clear winners. In 2027 we are much more versatile, and that will certainly affect our tactical approach in races, too,” said Tim Meeusen, Red Bull’s director of development. “But the goal remains the same: to develop our talents and bring them to the WorldTour.”

That means Hincapie is now one step behind the WorldTour squad. Two other Red Bull Rookies also signed pro contracts for 2027, so six out of 13 riders will race pro next season.

Budding superstar Finn also raced on the U19 squad and two years on Red Bull’s Rookies before graduating to the WorldTour in 2027 .

Hincapie will have a few years to race at the U23 level, but those are good odds.

The other big U.S. signing is Klau, who signs with Red Bull’s U19 squad grenke-Auto Eder after racing in 2026 on Hot Tubes, one of the top junior teams in the U.S.

Hot Tubes’ alumni list includes WorldTour stars like Magnus Sheffield, AJ August, Artem Shmidt, and Matteo Jorgenson.

Klau also got a taste of European racing this year with USA Cycling’s junior team, with a top 20 at the Course de la Paix Juniors, before a knee injury kept him out of nationals.

“An injury brought my road season to an early end, which definitely wasn’t part of the plan, but it’s also been a year that’s taught me a lot and given me plenty to take forward,” Klau wrote on Instagram.

Talent recruiters saw enough to make Klau one of six new signings on a 12-rider junior squad for 2027. The team also launched a cyclocross program this winter.

It’s a long way from a junior team to the WorldTour, but being inside Red Bull’s structure will give him a good shot.

The promotions also come after a quiet transfer season for the Red Bull WorldTour team.

After signing Evenepoel for 2026, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe’s only outside transfer for 2027 is Georg Steinhauser from EF Education-EasyPost. The four Rookies getting the bump to the WorldTour squad are Red Bull’s only other 2026-27 market moves.

That makes Klau and Hincapie as the first Americans to be tapped by Red Bull’s cutting-edge development teams.

Like most other major WorldTour operations, Red Bull is betting big on its internal talent program to discover its next generation of stars.

So having two Americans in the pipeline confirms that U.S. prospects are getting noticed by some of Europe’s biggest teams.

Could these two someday races alongside Evenepoel in the WorldTour?

Maybe. At least they’ll start in the pole position.

items.title: State Has a $1,500 Gravel Bike With Real Progressive Geometry and Big Tire Clearance
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The alloy bike brings tons of value to modern gravel dimensions, while State has improved some of its more finicky budget components.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Today, State is launching the 6061 All-Road V2, and it packs a ton of value into an alloy frame. Of course, the price jumps out as the biggest draw, but the bike also brings 55mm of clearance, improved componentry, and truly progressive geometry. Progressive geometry that many big brands say they provide, yet ultimately don’t quite hit.

For State, this new geometry is built around stability and traction, complete with a slightly slacker headtube angle, a long 445mm chainstay length, and a 73mm bottom bracket drop. State also tweaks the geometry on a size-by-size basis, which aims to maintain similar handling across the size run. Crucially, for the smaller sizes, this size-based geometry is designed to reduce toe overlap—even for 55mm tires on a 48cm frame.

The 6061 All-Road v2 is firmly pitched as a budget bike that brings costs down through components and materials, yet tries to bring quality through intentional design. That is where those aspects of geometry have come in.

Since the bike is not race-focused, that has given State the license to zero in on a geometry that boosts stability through the front and rear of the bike. Instead of packing big tires into a short chassis, State took a chance to push the expectations around head tube angle and chainstay length. This length, specifically the head tube angle ranging from 70-71.5 degrees and a 445 mm chainstay, is going to add stability—especially with the larger tires—and is designed to balance weight distribution for better traction. These attributes make a ton of sense for an entry-level bike.

Nevertheless, viewing this as an entry-level bike does do a bit of a disservice to how this bike could grow with a rider. From aspects like a T47 bottom bracket to relatively aero-shaped tubing with semi-internal cable routing, the bike could be upgraded easily.

Like all of State’s budget builds, part of how the brand finds savings is through building bikes with drivetrain components from outside of Shimano and SRAM. In the past, this has led to some, erm, creative component selection.

One of the most frustrating examples of this, in my experience, was a hybrid braking system that combined cable-actuated levers with a hydraulic caliper. It created one of the most disjointed, frustrating brake systems I have ever used, but it’s gone. On this new build, the system is a full flat-mount hydraulic system that should make for much more consistent and digestible riding.

There are still quirks like a Sensah SRX Pro 1×12 rear mech and a State-branded 42t crankset, but the frame is both UDH-compatible and has reasonable 165mm cranks for the smaller sizes and 170mm for the larger frames. The bike also comes with the option to run both 700c and 650b wheel sizes.

Lastly, speaking of those wheels, State has an in-house 700c wheel option that has an updated 25mm internal width, 32-spoke count rim to suit the wide 50mm Continental Hard Pack tires that come stock with the bike. There is also the option to upgrade to the DT Swiss G 1800 or the Zipp 303 S XPLR wheelset.

The State 6061 All-Road v2 is available in three colors—Liquid Emerald, Chrome Red, and Metallic Smoke—and four sizes. The builds start at $1,499, with add-ons including wheels, pedals, saddles, seatpost, and bottle cages.

For more information or to configure yours, visit State’s website .

items.title: ‘It Would Be Great to Win All Three’: Chloé Dygert Dreams of Gold Medal Sweep at the LA 2028 Olympics
items.author: ahood
items.content: Chloé Dygert confirms to Velo she will target gold in road and track at the LA 2028 Olympics after her return to US pro racing.
items.lbText:
Dygert, second from left, was part of the gold medal-winning team in Paris. (Photo: Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images)

Chloé Dygert may be leaving the WorldTour, but she’s keeping her foot on the accelerator with an ambitious target of three medals at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics .

Dygert told Velo she’s aiming to defend Team USA’s team pursuit title and chase the time trial and road race at LA 2028.

With the Games less than two years away, the 29-year-old is already building toward a possible gold medal trifecta that could make her one of the breakout stars in Los Angeles.

“Of course it would be great to win all three, the time trial for sure, and then the road race would be just a total bonus,” Dygert told Velo . “I gotta be realistic here, so winning the time trial and obviously coming back and winning the team pursuit would be huge.”

As one of America’s most successful Olympic cyclists , Dygert already owns four Olympic medals. She won team pursuit gold and time trial bronze at Paris 2024, adding to her team pursuit bronze from Tokyo 2020 and silver from Rio 2016.

Qualifying comes first. Then she has to hit her peak across two disciplines in the summer of 2028.

Speaking to Velo’s Hannah Knapp at El Tour de Tucson, Dygert was already putting down some training sessions on the outdoor track.

“So for how the Olympics works, it kind of goes by body count rather than like the event itself,” she said. “I’m for sure gonna do the track team pursuit as long as we qualify and then hopefully the time trial and then by doing the time trial, I have to do the road race, so I’ll be doing three events.”

Two medals in Paris, so why not three in Los Angeles?

Dygert’s road to Los Angeles will run through the United States.

This week she confirmed she’s returning to Virginia’s Blue Ridge TWENTY28 after six seasons with Canyon SRAM in the WorldTour.

Dygert has been through the wringer with injuries and health setbacks. Her time trial crash at the 2020 world championships in Imola, where she suffered a devastating injury to her left leg, still divides her career into before and after.

“I’ve spent my time in Europe and gave it the best shot that I could. Before my accident, that was the plan,” Dygert said. “I wanted to go to Europe and I wanted to win everything in Europe. I wanted to be the best in Europe.

“But because of the accident, unfortunately some of those goals got derailed. I think it was very obvious that I just was never going to be the athlete that I was before the accident.”

Dygert returns to Nicola Kramer’s Continental team where she raced as a junior a decade ago.

“So now it’s all about what do I do going forward, how do I make the best of who I can still be, and that is why I’ve decided to come back to America,” Dygert said.

“I’m coming back to something that I’m familiar with, coming back to a team that supports me and my goals,” she said. “I want to win the worlds. I want to win the Olympics, and I’ve done that before with her, and so what a better team to come back to.”

Dygert is one of USA Cycling’s best shots at gold on home roads in 2028.

The two-time world time trial champion took bronze against the clock in Paris, and she heads into the Los Angeles Olympics with a title to defend on the track and a third chance at a medal in the road race. Here’s how all three stack up.

1. Defend gold in the team pursuit Dygert has been at the heart of the U.S. team pursuit for three straight Olympics, with a medal each time and a breakthrough gold in Paris. She skipped the track worlds last month, but told Velo the pursuit is still front and center in her plans for LA28.

Team USA has work to do. The Americans finished ninth in qualifying at the Shanghai worlds, more than three seconds shy of advancing. Kristen Faulkner was the only rider from the Paris gold medal quartet on the start line in China.

Only eight teams will start in Los Angeles. Great Britain won gold in Shanghai ahead of Italy and Germany, a reminder of how deep the field is. The Americans will have to earn their place first.

If they can find their Paris speed again, they’ll be in the medal fight.

2. Win gold in the individual time trial This is her other big target.

Dygert has won two world time trial titles, and she was less than a second from Olympic silver on slick roads in Paris. Grace Brown was in a league of her own that day, beating Dygert by more than 90 seconds. Just 0.87 seconds separated Dygert from silver medalist Anna Henderson.

The course will matter. Organizers have confirmed a start at the LA Zoo and a finish at Griffith Observatory, with the full route still to come.

How much climbing comes before that finish could shape Dygert’s chances of turning bronze into gold.

3. Take a shot in the Olympic road race First, Dygert needs a spot on the road team.

The United States has two guaranteed road race places per gender as host and can earn up to four per gender through the UCI nations rankings.

The road race is the longest shot, but Dygert has the engine for a long, hard race in national colors.

She finished 31st in the Olympic road race in Tokyo and 15th in Paris. She was fourth in 2019 and second at the 2024 worlds in Zürich to show what she can do when she’s in the mix at the finish.

items.title: Polygon’s Fastest Gravel Bike To Date
items.author: Alison Jaksen
items.content: Want to go fast and explore far and wide? The new Tambora is built for top-end speed over changing terrain.
items.lbText:
Polygon's new Tambora gravel bike. (Photo: Polygon Bikes)

Since 1989, manufacturing and development has been in Polygon Bikes’ DNA. The Indonesia-based factory brand is in a country shaped by tremendous geological forces. The island nation’s massive volcanoes have reformed the landscape countless times and created awe-inspiring topography.

The lesson: Change is good. Polygon focused on a clear priority with the evolution of the all-new Tambora: speed. This is the fastest gravel bike the company has produced, with design elements that let riders push their routes faster and further than ever. Compared to the previous version of the Tambora, the front end is 32mm lower, while the head angle slackens by 0.8 degrees. Those tweaks improve aerodynamics for both bike and rider, while the longer wheelbase and chainstays create more stability when you’re charging down the trail.

​Adding to the Tambora’s race-ready performance: its frame. The frame’s ACX carbon-fiber construction takes inspiration from its Helios road bike sibling—designed to excel at power transfer while reducing ride fatigue. The bike also boasts 55c tire clearance and is compatible with 1x and 2x drivetrains. If more rugged terrain calls to you, the Tambora is also compatible with aftermarket suspension forks up to 40mm of travel, without changing the current geometry.

​While speed is this bike’s specialty, it also features the thoughtful, rider-friendly design elements Polygon is known for. The new Tambora takes full advantage of the brand’s PolyPocket internal frame storage, which offers a full downtube width opening for easy access. This soft-sided, zippered pouch holds tools, snacks, and other essentials in a convenient, low-profile package. Up in the cockpit, a Fidlock mount recessed into the top tube makes it quick and easy to connect your preferred accessories, while keeping everything tight when you ratchet up the RPMs.

Also great: The value proposition for Polygon Bikes is as good as the performance. The Tambora series starts at $1,799, with a wide range of competitively priced options. The Tambora 7 Di2 ($2,999) and Tambora 9 AXS with SRAM Force ($4,499) are particularly good deals considering the specs.

Put it all together and you have a bike that’s both fast and capable of serious saddle time—and comes at sweet price. With four models across six frame sizes, there’s a redesigned Tambora for every gravel rider who wants to experience the wonders of evolution for themselves.

Founded in 1989, Polygon began with a simple belief: Great bikes shouldn’t be out of reach. What started as a small OEM operation has grown through decades of building, experimenting, and refining bikes for real riders—experiences that still define the global brand today.

items.title: What the TotalEnergies Exit Means for Netcompany-Ineos
items.author: ahood
items.content: French company TotalEnergies is leaving its deal with Netcompany-Ineos to pivot into the women's peloton and back Demi Vollering.
items.lbText:
TotalEnergies is leaving Netcompany-Ineos in a pivot to women's racing. (Photo: ASPER JACOBS / BELGA MAG / Belga / AFP via Getty Images)

Netcompany-Ineos will lose TotalEnergies as a backer in 2027 just as the former Tour de France powerhouse tries to rebuild its challenge for the yellow jersey.

The departure — first reported by The Athletic and subsequently confirmed by the team — ends a partnership that began ahead of the 2025 Tour. The French energy giant reportedly contributed more than €10 million annually.

That leaves a major hole to fill, but the team did not say reveal the exit will affect its budget.

“We’re grateful to everyone at TotalEnergies for their support and commitment since joining us ahead of the 2025 Tour de France. They’ve been valued partners, and we’re proud to have represented the TotalEnergies brand across two seasons of racing,” a Netcompany-Ineos spokesperson said in a statement to the media.

It’s a financial hit as the team is undergoing a rebuilding effort to regain its spot in the Tour de France conversation.

Danish technology company Netcompany joined as title sponsor in May, reportedly worth around €20 million per season. Ineos remains the team owner and has been searching for new financial partners to help ease the financial cost of the WorldTour team.

Team officials did not reveal how this will impact the team’s budget for 2027.

The team saw high turnover during this year’s transfer season, with Filippo Ganna, Ben Turner, Andrew August, Magnus Sheffield, and Artem Shimdt among several riders leaving.

Though there were no marquee signings, it picked up highly touted junior world champion Benjamín Noval and Riley Sheehan among nine new arrivals for 2027.

At its peak, during the Sky/Ineos era, it won seven Tours with eight different riders from 2012 to 2019, but has not reached the Paris podium since Geraint Thomas finished third in 2022.

Expected race leader Oscar Onley missed this year’s race due to a shoulder injury, and Egan Bernal’s 20th was the team’s top GC.

TotalEnergies, meanwhile, is pivoting its cycling resources into women’s racing .

It exited Jean-René Bernaudeau’s men’s ProTeam squad, which lated landed replacement sponsor XEFI for three seasons through 2029.

This week, the French company also committed to five seasons as co-title title sponsor of Demi Vollering’s team from 2027.

The squad will race as Team TotalEnergies-FDJ United through 2031.

items.title: Giro d’Italia Taps MAAP to Make the Pink Jersey in 2027
items.author: ahood
items.content: MAAP will design the Giro's 'maglia rosa' in 2027 as Castelli replaces Santini at the Tour de France and Vuelta in grand tour leader's jersey reshuffle.
items.lbText:
MAAP is linking up with the Giro d'Italia in bold new deal. (Photo: Gruber Images/MAAP)

MAAP will make and design the Giro d’Italia’s pink jersey in 2027 in a big move for the Melbourne company that built its name on minimalist graphics and high-end performance.

The multi-year agreement with RCS Sport includes the classification jerseys at the Giro d’Italia , Giro d’Italia Women and Giro Next Gen, including the iconic maglia rosa .

“MAAP was founded in Melbourne just 12 years ago. In 2027, we’ll design the ‘maglia rosa,'” cofounder Jarrad Smith said in the announcement. “It’s the race that got me into road cycling.”

MAAP will also supply technical apparel for all RCS races, in both men’s and women’s editions at Strade Bianche, Milano-Sanremo, Il Lombardia, Tirreno-Adriatico, Giro-E, Milano-Torino, Il Giro d’Abruzzo, and GranPiemonte.

Financial terms were not disclosed Thursday when officials confirmed the deal.

MAAP built a following among younger cyclists with its trademark graphics and street-wear cred coupled with top-end performance quality.

The company quickly grew organically and was built by word of mouth into what’s now a global brand.

For RCS, the pivot comes as the Italian grand tour is trying to get younger fans to start adding the Giro into their social media feeds.

“We are confident that the new jerseys, which will be unveiled soon, will generate great interest among all cycling fans, and particularly among younger generations,” said Paolo Bellino, CEO and general manager of RCS Sports and Events.

No one knows. Thursday’s announcement only confirmed the deal.

“The partnership seeks to bridge the deep traditions of European racing with contemporary culture through performance and design,” a statement read.

Based on the PR, it also sounds like there will be special-edition apparel and accessories for each race via “race capsules.”

The first jerseys will be revealed ahead of Milano-Sanremo in March.

The Giro’s switch is part of a leader’s jersey reshuffle across all three grand tours.

Castelli , which supplied the Giro’s pink jersey through this year, will replace Santini at both the Tour de France and the Vuelta a España in 2027.

The Tour is reviving the Castelli partnership that dates back to the days of Greg LeMond and Miguel Indurain in a deal that ran from 1989 to 1994.

The Giro and MAAP link up after the brand worked with the GreenEdge organization and Jayco-AlUla starting in 2025.

Its Pro Aero race suit has been part of stage wins at all three men’s grand tours, the Tour de France Femmes, and a string of WorldTour classics.

Now it will hit the podium every day across the RCS Sport race portfolio.

items.title: The Avinox Motor Disrupted e-MTB. Now It’s Coming for Your Commute.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Amflow expands beyond the trail with the carbon UE Series, pairing 125 Nm of torque with electronic shifting and integrated tech for city riding.
items.lbText:
This week, Amflow is expanding beyond electric mountain bikes with the launch of its first city commuter line, the Amflow UE Series. On the surface, it sounds like yet another unfamiliar name offering a high-powered commuter bike, but the news is a bit bigger than that. What this really means is that DJI-backed Amflow and its Avinox motor are making the jump from e-MTB to city riding.

Available now in the UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro builds, the platform pairs that drive system with a claimed 2.35-kilogram full-carbon, low step-through frame to hit a complete bike weight of 20.9 kilograms, or roughly 46 pounds. It makes for an impressive offering on paper and raises the obvious question of whether putting that kind of hardware into a transportation-focused package will reshape the commuter market the same way Amflow did e-MTB.

Rather than offering a traditional multi-size run at launch, Amflow designed the standard UE frame to accommodate riders between 5 feet, 1 inch and 6 feet, 3 inches using two interchangeable stem heights. A dedicated small frame for riders between 4 feet, 7 inches and 5 feet, 3 inches is scheduled to arrive in 2027.

Beyond that, the bike follows expected commuter design patterns, leaning toward comfort and visibility. The first lever of that focus is frame geometry, starting with a step-through frame and flat handlebars to put the rider in an upright position. That layout is paired with 65 mm of front suspension, a seatpost with 125 mm of height adjustment and 30 mm of suspension travel, and wide 26×2.0-inch Maxxis tires. Braking comes from Magura 180 mm disc brakes with three-finger levers. For hauling cargo, Amflow equips the bike with a front rack rated for 20 kilograms (about 44 pounds) and a rear MIK HD-compatible rack rated for 27 kilograms (about 59.5 pounds).

The biggest news here is that the motor that disrupted the e-MTB market is expanding into new territory. Powering both builds is the Avinox M2 drive unit, which Amflow claims delivers up to 125 Nm of torque and an 8-to-1 maximum assist ratio. According to the brand, the motor can climb 30% grades under load while keeping operating noise below 45 dBA. The system also includes a traction control feature and a new Auto Boost mode that automatically increases power output on steep hills or loaded starts without rider input.

Both builds use a removable 600Wh battery, with Amflow claiming a maximum range of 132 kilometers (about 82 miles) under controlled testing conditions. It charges from zero to 100% in 2 hours and 23 minutes, and riders can set a custom charge limit to preserve cell longevity.

Both models also feature electronic shifting with automatic and smooth-shifting modes, leaving the drivetrain as the main mechanical difference between the two. The UE Carbon Pro uses a custom three-speed electronic internal geared hub paired with a Gates carbon belt, which allows riders to shift while stopped and avoids chain maintenance or greasy clothes — though it costs more. Alternatively, the less expensive Amflow UE Carbon uses a 10-speed electronic rear derailleur co-developed with TRP.

Amflow leans heavily into its connected ecosystem on the UE Series, integrating several new Avinox accessories directly into the bike. Control centers on a 1.4-inch DP200 handlebar touchscreen paired with a rotating phone mount that offers 15W wireless and 20W USB-C charging. The integrated lighting system features automatic dusk activation, high- and low-beam switching and a brake-sensing rear light.

Through the Avinox Ride app, riders can pair multiple bikes to one account, merge ride files, sync with an Apple Watch and control compatible DJI Osmo cameras from the handlebar. The system can also pair with a heart rate monitor to adjust motor assist automatically based on a target heart rate zone.

On the security front, a single key operates both the battery lock and an integrated 10 mm hardened steel ART 2-Star horseshoe lock. The bike also supports Apple Find My tracking and an app-based Lost Mode designed to disable the bike remotely if it is stolen.

Both the Amflow UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro are available immediately through Amflow’s website and authorized dealers. U.S. pricing is $3,499 for the UE Carbon and $3,899 for the UE Carbon Pro.
