items.title: 24 Top Cycling Teams Are Making A New Money Move To Fix Cycling’s Business Model
items.author: ahood
items.content: Two dozen teams join forces in a new venture to try to create untapped revenue streams to help underwrite today's super team budgets. Can they fix cycling's business model?
items.lbText:
Teams are floating a new project to collectively sell what they bring to the peloton. (Photo: Loic VENANCE / AFP via Getty Images)

Top pro teams are taking another stab at trying to fix cycling’s business model.

Some 24 squads are forming a company designed to turn their collective commercial muscle into new revenue steams.

Collective Cycling Group Ltd. (CCG), a UK-based business owned by participating teams, announced a shareholder agreement including teams from the men’s and women’s WorldTour and ProTeam ranks.

Discussions with additional teams are ongoing, a statement confirmed Wednesday.

“Teams carry much of the sporting and financial risk in professional cycling, while many of the sport’s commercial opportunities remain fragmented,” CCG director Oliver Ciesla said in the announcement. “The UCI reform process creates a first opportunity to address these challenges together.”

Instead of making a run directly at TV rights, which are controlled by races, teams are looking at what they bring to the table in the form of cycling’s biggest stars.

The idea is to bundle what they have into something bigger that fans, broadcasters, and sponsors might be interested in paying money for.

That includes team commercial rights, data, media content, merchandising, hospitality, and fan experiences.

The end game is to give teams a stronger financial footing rather than leaving them constantly chasing the next sponsor and relying almost exclusively on sponsorship backing to underwrite ever-rising team budgets.

The announcement follows the stalled ONE Cycling project , which died on the vine after the UCI rejected it in June 2025 .

Corporate filings show CCG previously operated under the name OneCycling Limited, according to Reuters .

The release doesn’t mention a new racing series or a call for shared broadcast revenues.

Instead, the focus is on developing commercial opportunities around assets the teams already hold.

They hope to organize their newest project as part of the UCI’s ongoing Project 2030 effort to reshape professional road cycling.

The announcement does not identify the 24 teams, disclose financial commitments, or set a timetable for its first products.

Cycling’s tried this before. Let’s see if something will change.

items.title: Testing the Tech and Heat Training Required to Survive a 95-Degree Tour de France
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: From Q36.5 cooling apparel to physiological heat blocks, we stepped into a climate chamber to find out what it really takes to combat extreme temperatures.
items.lbText:
There is a giant vault in Bolzano, Italy that can simulate elevation higher than Mount Everest, a freeze as cold as Siberia, and temperatures so hot that they are used to help train firefighters. On October 21, I stepped into that vault wearing nothing but a cycling kit and shoes.

As I swung my leg over a stationary bike, the fans revved up in front of me as the chamber adjusted its climate to match Stage 2 of this year’s Tour de France. It was a hot day in Barcelona when Isaac del Toro won ahead of Tadej Pogacar and Remco Evenepoel. By the end of the Tour, it was the hottest race on record with an average temperature of 32.4°C (90.3°F) across the 21 stages.

Excessive heat usually means a decline in performance. But with the advent of heat training, cooling strategies, and ever-improving clothing technology, professional cyclists are faster than ever, even during the hottest Tour de France in history.

The moment I stepped into the vault — the TerraX Cube — I knew what was at stake. I was here alongside the CORE team and more than 20 other journalists to test the new Q36.5 Gregarius Pro Evo Jersey, Base Layer Subzero, and Dottore Pro Bib Shorts. The vault was set to 35°C (95°F) degrees with a humidity of 50%, far from the ideal temperature to achieve peak performance. I had just done a heat training session in CORE’s Sweatlab, so I had a baseline of data for what I could expect as my core temperature rose.

Not only were we going to ride in excessive heat, we were going to simulate the finale of Stage 2 of the Tour using a custom workout on Zwift. Here was the workout , along with my power targets based on my FTP:

I was already dripping sweat during the warmup thanks to the ambient temperature, and my sweat rate intensified as my power increased to 360w. After a quick recovery, we began the hardest part of the test (in my opinion): four minutes at VO2 Max in 95-degree heat. This is the type of effort short enough that you can maintain an output above threshold, but long enough that your heart rate and RPE will be jacked up by the end of the effort.

The final few intervals went by fast as I could see the metaphorical finish line in front of me. And just like that, it was all over. CORE gathered data from our body temperature sensors, and we shuffled our way into the cool hallway. The testing was over; now it was time to look at the results.

To my surprise, our performances in the heat chamber didn’t drop off significantly. In fact, many riders (myself included) performed at their best despite the hot conditions. This was a sharp contrast to my data from CORE’s Sweatlab where I pushed myself to the limit without ever breaking 300w.

The lab test at CORE – done two days before the test in Bolzano – was a data-gathering mission. I wasn’t there to chase power PBs or set an impressive time. I was there to sweat; and that I did.

During the normal cooling conditions, I wore a cycling kit and had two fans pointed towards me. I was riding on a Zwift Ride with ERG mode turned on, so my power output was steady to the Watt. The initial 15-minute interval established the baseline where my heart rate was steady at 138 bpm, and my core temperature stabilized at 38°C (100.4°F).

The hard part was up next: 35 minutes of heat training. That meant pulling on the CORE heat training suit, turning the fans off, and turning the heater on. Within minutes, my sweat started pooling on the floor. Over the course of 35 minutes, my heart rate rose from 138 bpm to 175 bpm without any change in power. I rode at 280w the entire time, but it felt like I was doing a threshold interval for the last 15 minutes.

That is the damage that heat can do to your performance. Without sufficient cooling, Zone 2 power can feel like Zone 4 power once your heat strain reaches a certain level. That was the kind of performance degradation that CORE was looking for in the Italian climate cube. But the closer they looked at the results, the more they realized that the clothing had worked.

We were all wearing Q36.5 kit in the climate chamber, specifically designed for use in 30°C+ (86°F) heat. Tom Pidcock loves heat training, and it was no surprise to hear that he plays a major role in the R&D of Q36.5 kit. (Fun fact: he’s also the only rider on Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling Team who wears an XXS skinsuit.)

As I pored through my own performance data, I remembered how good my legs felt during the final two-minute interval in the heat chamber. Despite feeling hot, my body had performed extremely well in the conditions. Personally, that is the biggest difference that I’ve noticed after doing a heat training block.

Without heat acclimatization, my body has typically reacted to the heat like it did in CORE’s Sweatlab. My heart rate would rise uncontrollably as my legs are drained of their strength. But after a big heat training block, I noticed that I could still hit my best power numbers in excessively hot conditions. Not only would my heart rate be 10 bpm lower than expected, but it would stabilize during long efforts in the heat – quite the opposite of what I experienced in the CORE Sweatlab.

One of my biggest takeaways was that the clothing had worked. This wasn’t the only heat adaptation method that I asked Q36.5 and CORE about during this trip. I also asked about cold drinks, pouring water over your head, rubbing ice cubes on your wrists, and of course, heat training. Let’s start with what does work.

Cold drinks and gels are probably the most effective ways to cool your body from the inside out. When you’re talking about performance degradation in the heat, you are most often talking about an increase in core temperature as well as an increase in skin temperature. This is known as heat strain, something that CORE quantifies with their sensor and app, and the key metric that many riders use for heat training.…

items.title: Primož Roglič Lands a Contract to Join NSN Cycling for 2027
items.author: ahood
items.content: Roglič signs late-hour deal with NSN Cycling for 2027 that will keep the popular Slovenian in the WorldTour for at least one more season.
items.lbText:
Roglič joins NSN on a one-year deal. (Photo: Marco BERTORELLO / AFP via Getty Images)

Primož Roglič will race in 2027 and will join NSN Cycling on a one-year deal.

In a late-hour move, the deal means the 37-year-old Slovenian will be in the WorldTour peloton next season.

“I always like challenges,” Roglič said in a team note. “That’s why I’m here, to take these on together and see what the future brings us.

“It took me some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never. It feels like the perfect connection.”

Roglič, one of the superstars over the past decade, was looking down the barrel at possible retirement at the end of 2026.

Talks with several teams ended without a signature , but things came together quickly with NSN Cycling.

“From the first moment we spoke, it was evident that Primož still has a lot of passion for the sport and a drive to be the best he can,” said NSN Cycling general manager Kjell Carlström. “It was an easy decision to make.”

The former ski jumper ended his three-year run with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe after a season that included second overall at the Vuelta a España and a win at the European time trial championship.

It was more of a question if he wanted to keep racing and at what price.

Roglič was sometimes bizarrely ambivalent in his public statements about his future, but he was talking with several teams behind the scenes.

Talks petered out, however, with one team after another. NSN offered a one-year contract but no financial details were revealed.

Roglič was reportedly earning around $3 million a year with Red Bull, so a high asking price might have been a factor on some teams taking a pass on the veteran.

Roglič — a winner of five grand tours — will link up with Richard Carapaz, Santiago Buitrago, and Lennert Van Eetvelt on the reinvigorated NSN lineup.

“This signing reflects the ambition we have for the future. We want to compete at the highest level, challenge for major results and continue building a team capable of achieving great things,” Carlström said. “We are confident that Primož can play an important role in that journey, and we look forward to seeing him race in NSN colors.”

Roglič scored nearly 1,000 UCI points in 2026 , something that will come in handy if he can repeat it next season for NSN Cycling.

The team — formerly Israel-Premier Tech — finished ranked 19th in the rolling three-year WorldTour rankings, one spot out of the guaranteed top 18 licenses.

There’s no news yet on a possible calendar, but at NSN he should see plenty of chances to race.

“I still believe I have some work to do, in both racing and with myself,” Roglič said. “I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things.”

The team broke the news on social media, with a smiling Roglič using a “like and follow” of the team’s social media channel.

Roglič — who was beaten by Tadej Pogačar at the wild TT finale at the 2020 Tour de France — will join his new teammates at a winter camp in Spain next month.

items.title: Seixas, Pidcock, Kuss: Who Stays and Who Goes in 2027?
items.author: ahood
items.content: Paul Seixas, Tom Pidcock, and Sepp Kuss headline riders out of contract in 2027 as teams start shopping early for the talent to take on Pogačar.
items.lbText:
Seixas will be the center of transfer intrigue in 2027. (Photo: Anne-Christine POUJOULAT / AFP)

Everyone wants Paul Seixas . In 2027, they might get their chance.

Seixas’ contract expires after next season, and the mad scramble for his contract is already starting to rumble.

He’s not alone. Tom Pidcock , Sepp Kuss , and Lenny Martinez are the other marquee names off-contract in 2027 who will be headlining next year’s high-stakes transfer market.

A few riders are still looking for spots in 2027 after their deals ran out this year, including Primož Roglič and Max Schachmann, among a dozen others.

For everyone else, attention is already shifting to the 2027-28 transfer season, which could rival last year’s upheaval , when Remco Evenepoel, Juan Ayuso and Oscar Onley all ripped up existing deals and swapped jerseys.

Tadej Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard are both under contract and secure at the top of the hierarchy. For anyone else hoping to catch up, a few big names could make the difference.

For this year, it’s going to be all about the Seixas Sweepstakes. And what he does will shape the entire market .

The gossip will start at the team camps next month in Spain and be hyped by leaks, exclusives, and conjecture all the way to the Tour de France.

Here are the big transfer names to watch in 2027:

There won’t be a bigger transfer saga in 2027 than Paul Seixas. And there might not be a bigger price tag, either, if this year’s $13 million rumored offer comes true.

The 20-year-old French phenom more than proved his quality in a rock-solid WorldTour campaign, becoming the youngest-ever winner of Il Lombardia and nearly hitting the podium in his Tour de France debut with fourth overall.

He’s the top name off-contract in 2027, and nearly every team has reached out . Visma-Lease a Bike and Pinarello Q36.5 are already circling, with Q36.5 reportedly putting a massive €13 million per year on the table for 2028.

There’s talk Seixas could target victory at the Giro d’Italia in May rather than return to a less favorable Tour route and another July trying to hold Pogačar’s wheel.

The bigger question is whether Decathlon can convince him to stay beyond 2027.

The team is certainly trying. It has recruited more stage racing support, notably Pavel Sivakov, to give its franchise rider more company when the road kicks up.

Seixas seems happy at Decathlon and has chosen to honor his final year of his current deal . That buys the team another few months to prove he can chase cycling’s biggest prizes without changing jerseys.

With suitors lining up, the ball is in his court. Seixas could name his price and take his pick, but salary might not settle this one.

Can Decathlon give him everything he needs in coaching, training, nutrition, equipment, and aerodynamics to match the super teams?

Keeping Seixas will take more than paying him like a Tour winner. The deciding factor will be if Decathlon can convince him he can become one there.

Visma will have nearly half its roster out of contract at the end of 2027, so the team will be busy locking down its leaders and shopping for fresh legs.

One rider it probably won’t have to worry about losing is Sepp Kuss. It’s hard to imagine the “Eagle of Durango” in any other jersey.

Kuss is a team anchor, a huge fan favorite, and the last American to win a grand tour with his 2023 Vuelta a España victory.

Fans might still want more “GC Kuss,” and Visma knows how valuable he is.

Kuss is essential to the Killer Bees ethos. Across the team’s latest run of grand tour success, he has been part of every winning lineup except Simon Yates’ 2025 Giro d’Italia squad.

And he’s still putting numbers on the board, including a Giro stage win to complete the “grand tour” sweep of stages, and finishing fifth at the Vuelta.

Kuss admits he doesn’t like the pressure of leadership, so he probably won’t be chasing a big-money contract to be a GC leader on another team.

The bigger question might be how much longer Kuss wants to keep doing it.

A recent at-home video offered a glimpse of a happy life in Andorra with his wife and child. So far, there’s no hint he’s ready to trade mountain passes for more afternoons at home. His favored program of racing all three grand tours also fits his work-life balance.

If both sides want it, a “forever” contract like those signed by Wout van Aert and Marianne Vos would seem a fitting way to keep him in yellow and black.

It’s equally hard to imagine Pidcock going anywhere else.

His blockbuster move to Pinarello Q36.5 was one of the top transfers two years ago.

Since then, Pidcock’s more than earned his spot as the team’s franchise rider. Perhaps 2026 was missing one big win, but taking Pogačar to the line at Milan-San Remo, another mountain bike world title, and a top 10 in the Tour de France confirmed his chops.

Pinarello Q36.5 remains one of the most aggressive teams on the rider market , picking up 10 new riders coming into 2027.

Doug Ryder, with the backing of team owners, is pushing the pedal for WorldTour classification by the next round at the end of 2028.

For Pidcock, his spot is secure, so it will be a question of hammering out the details on how many zeroes are attached to his next deal.

The team gives him the schedule he likes, plus carves out time for his MTB side quest. With the LA Olympic Games coming up, Pidcock won’t be wanting to swap teams.

Unless someone can convince him otherwise.

If it weren’t for Seixas, Lenny Martinez would have finished the 2026 Tour de France as the top French rider, in fifth.

That will give him some bargaining power coming into 2027.

At 23, his stock is still rising, even if Seixas has grabbed the spotlight as France’s next great Tour hope.

The son of Olympic mountain bike champion Miguel Martinez and grandson of Tour king of the mountains winner Mariano Martinez has the family pedigree. The consistency is still lacking, but the first half of 2026 confirmed his potential.…

items.title: Velo Poll: Should the Men’s Tour de France Add ‘Hommes’?
items.author: ahood
items.content: Marlen Reusser wants equal billing for the Tour de France and its women’s edition. Keep tradition or change the names? Have your say in our poll.
items.lbText:
Should the men's Tour de France also be called 'Hommes'? (Photo: Gruber Images)

There’s the Tour de France and the Tour de France Femmes . Should the men’s race carry “Hommes” for equal billing?

The Swiss star wants “Hommes” added to the men’s Tour if the women’s edition carries “Femmes,” arguing that cycling’s language still treats men as the default and women as the supporting act.

“I don’t want to be a decoration of a male sport,” she told the Domestique Hotseat podcast.

That question is timely as more races hold both men’s and women’s editions.

What’s the best way to name paired events?

Is adding one word a step toward equal billing? Or should the Tour keep its historic name?

Reusser also floated another idea of having the UCI require matching names across men’s and women’s events.

ASO , meanwhile, seems reluctant to change its brand name after more than 100 years of history in the men’s race.

Vote in our latest Velo Poll below and tell us whether the men’s Tour needs to change its name.

items.title: Why SBT GRVL Is Challenging Another Race Over Four Letters
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: A post about SBT GRVL’s email to Rez Gravel regarding the GRVL trademark protection has gone viral
items.lbText:
SBT GRVL has been embroiled in online controversy after an uproar over the brand’s enforcement of a trademark around the term GRVL.

It all started with an Instagram post. @rezgravel on Instagram, the page representing an Indigenous-led community gravel event in Sacaton, Arizona, posted an email they received from SBT GRVL requesting that Rez Gravel stop using the term GRVL in marketing materials around the event.

The Rez Gravel post was a protest of that email. The post comment highlighted the lack of infrastructure around the Rez Gravel event, how the email from SBT would force them to spend money they don’t have on new posters and a logo redesign, and criticism of the lack of care and consideration SBT GRVL showed in denying their request for comped entry into SBT GRVL for native riders in the past.

That post generated over a thousand likes and hundreds of comments, with many people criticizing SBT GRVL, bringing into question the viability of a trademark of the term GRVL, and supporting the Indigenous-led event and organization.

On Sunday, November 15th, Rez Gravel posted a screenshot of an email the race received from SBT GRVL around the use of the GRVL term on previous marketing material for their January 9th and 10th community bike rides.

“So I guess @sbtgrvl owns ‘GRVL’ and we’ll have to stop using GRVL,” the caption under Rez Gravel’s post read. “SBT GRVL introduced me to gravel cycling when I was an @rideforracialjustice RFRJ athlete in 2022. In the past, I have been one of SBT GRVL’s biggest supporters. I returned to SBT GRVL in 2023, 2024 and in 2023 even went halfway around the world to support their race @fnldgrvl FNLD GRVL in Finland.

“I tried to bring a Native Gravel team to SBT GRVL in 2024. I tried to ask Amy, Ryan, and Greer for free or even discounted entry as a way to honor the First Nations people, including my cousin from the Ute Indian Tribe- Uintah and Ouray Reservation, whose people were removed from the land in the area now known as Steamboat Springs. Amy and her team refused to honor native people with even a reduced-fee entry for my cousin in 2024.”

And then came the crux of their argument.

“Rez Gravel does not use the GRVL in our LLC, DBA, or website names. Rez Gravel does not sell any merchandise that uses the GRVL name or logo. Rez Gravel is owned by a Gila River Indian Community tribal member and solely operates on the Gila River Indian Community a Sovereign Nation.

“Rez Gravel only has an annual revenue of around $4,000, and after expenses only about 2,000-3,000 keeps our community bike shop going for the year. The posters are printed for 2027 and out of money until some more funds come in from 2027 Registration.”

A second post from the Rez Gravel organization a day later added to that online discourse, with the organization posting details of the federally registered trademarks that SBT GRVL invoked in their emails and a caption that articulated how the Rez Gravel organization was not infringing upon the two separate trademarks that SBT GRVL has around the term GRVL.

In total, SBT GRVL has trademarks on the terms SBT GRVL, FNLD GRVL, RADL GRVL, and two specific trademarks around the term GRVL. One of those terms covers cycling events, while the other protects the use of GRVL for merchandise.

In the case of Rez Gravel, SBT GRVL didn’t specify which trademark they were invoking—they did not have to since the email was a courtesy note and not a formal cease—but it is likely the trademark around the event.

In an exclusive interview with Velo , the SBT GRVL organizers explained the reason behind the email and their trademarks.

“It was back a few years ago that we decided that we needed to trademark the event,” Amy Charity, the SBT GRVL race director, told Velo.

“We had established a brand, and we knew that SBT GRVL stood for something that we were really proud of. We were a safe event, an event that was inclusive, an event that was credible and professional.

“At the time, we were also considering expanding our brand by putting on events such as FNLND GRVL or RADL GRVL. In doing so, we wanted to ensure that the riders, the participants, and the sponsors would know what they were getting—when you hear GRVL, when you see GRVL, there’s a standard that you associate with what we will uphold and what we’ll honor.”

Like all trademark processes, that trademark process took many months to complete with the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). In that process, to get the trademarks for the term GRVL, SBT GRVL had to both prove distinctiveness and prove they were using the trademark to identify their brand to consumers.

Additionally, as with all trademark or copyright instances, SBT GRVL had to demonstrate they were actively using the trademark for commercial use, and that they are actively enforcing their intellectual property if they deem that trademark has been violated.

That has meant that each time an event has used the GRVL distinction since, they have been required by law to notify the brand that is using their trademarked term.

“The very first time it happened, it was because there was confusion in the marketplace,” Ryan Steers, SBT GRVL’s Marketing Director, told Velo. “We had a sponsor approach us and say, we didn’t know that you were putting on an event in a different country, and asked why we didn’t tell them we were doing it and why they weren’t the first that you approached.

“It was confusing, especially in our market, particularly because it was a US-based company putting on an international event with GRVL in the title. So we reached out to that event business and said, ‘Hey, we wanted to give you a heads-up, we own the trademark for GRVL as it relates to events.’

“That’s what we do when we see an event out there related to gravel cycling that has been using GRVL. There have been around three events that we’ve reached out to.”…

items.title: 2026 Rouleur Live Tech Gallery: Chinese Tech, Titanium Splendor, and Everything In Between
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: From new Chinese race bikes, to beautiful titanium creations, here are our favorites from the tech show at Rouleur Live.
items.lbText:
This Titanium Chiru Aerix caught my eye for similar reasons. Although in this case, the frame design is much more modern - especially given the quite lengthy headtube. (Photo: Ties Wijntjes/Velo)

This weekend, London was the host for the 2026 Rouleur Live . Although it is not the biggest show, there are plenty of beautiful bikes, bespoke frames, and even some new tech.

Rouleur Live has been on my wish list to attend for several years, and this year I finally made it out to the London-based show. I think there is no event in cycling quite like Rouleur Live. It combines live interviews with some of pro cycling’s greatest stars such as Mathieu van der Poel, Lotte Kopecky and Mads Pedersen, with a relatively small but tech-packed expo.

Besides that and maybe even more importantly, it is also known as the unofficial end-of-year celebration for the British bike industry. I am no Brit, but considering the vicinity of many different pubs around the show and the British knack for throwing a party, I felt quite compelled to finally attend the show this year.

Luckily, it did not disappoint on any of those aspects. In the industrial atmosphere of the Truman Brewery, many of cycling’s most renowned brands were present. With relatively little space, many brands made the most of what they had and brought out some of their fanciest, newest, and most fascinating tech.

Surprisingly, there were even some new products on display, which is not always a given at Rouleur considering the time of year. One brand representative managed to summarize what most exhibitors were showcasing pretty well: brands were celebrating this year’s achievements, or teasing next year’s novelties.

Besides, with an Italian pavilion and many British bespoke brands attending too, there was more than enough to feast the eyes on. Let’s dive into our tech gallery of one of the last bike shows of the season.

items.title: 13 Holiday Gifts for Gravel Cyclist for Every Type of Budget
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: Gravel cycling requires a lot of gear, but we kept it simple. Here is a short, expert-tested list of equipment every off-road rider actually wants.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Welcome to Velo Deals. We sift through the retail landscape to bring you deals worth paying attention to. It might be a discount or it might just be a product so good you should grab it. Either way, if it’s worth your time, you’ll see it here. If you’d like to see the rest of the category, check all our Velo Deals coverage.

Finding the right gear for the gravel cyclist in your life is notoriously difficult—mostly because their wish list never ends. Fortunately, we at Velo spend the entire year testing this equipment, so we know exactly what they actually need for a new year of adventures.

To help get the right gear into the right hands, I have put together a curated list of thirteen top-tier gravel gifts. This list covers a broad price range, features items that will impress even the rider who has it all, and includes a few deals to save you some cash along the way.

The Wolf Tooth DEL pedals are a piece of kit I cannot recommend enough—they are one of the few things I never ride gravel without. I use both the standard-issue alloy version and the premium Mark Zero titanium models. Both offer massive upside, making mountain bike shoes feel as efficient as road shoes on the flats, while remaining fully capable in mud, dirt, and ice.

Speaking of gravel staples, most of my rides with those pedals have been done in the Quoc Gran Tourer XC shoes. I have long been a fan of Quoc’s dedicated off-road line, and that hasn’t changed with this slightly stiffer XC version. While they might lack some of the hyper-stiffness of dedicated cross-country race shoes, the Gran Tourer is a 10/10 on the comfort scale and has proven to be incredibly durable. They are the perfect companion for everything from a three-hour adventure ride to a multi-day bikepacking trip.

Bikepacking is one of those things that people rarely do just once. If you are up for one trip, you’ll be up for the next one. A great rear rack only makes that more certain, and there are no rear racks quite like Tailfin. The only knock on Tailfin up until now has been the price. With the Journey Pannier Rack, the UK-based adventure brand finally has something at a lower price point. Now, you can get the same mix of functionality and craftsmanship that Tailfin has refined from working with the best ultra-riders in the world at a much-reduced price.

If you ride gravel, chances are you have been “darked on”—caught out too late without enough light to get you home. The Exposure Lights Sirius front light is built so this never happens again. This small light is brighter than it looks, easy to charge, and with the right mount, it stows safely out of the way to keep modern cockpits looking clean. Its industrial design adds a bit of bling to your setup, blending high-end functionality with a slick metallic aesthetic.

I never ride without a Dynaplug tool. For five years now, I have brought at least one of these small tools to fix flats on road, mountain, and gravel rides. It has saved me on a bikepacking trip through Ecuador and while road riding around my neighborhood. It doesn’t fix every flat, but dang, it will fix a lot of them. Most of that riding has been done with the exact same Dynaplug Racer Pro tool. So while the price seems high for one small tool, it is well worth it for any rider—especially gravel cyclists.

The Lezyne E-Drive pump has been an effective travel companion for me this year. It lets you inflate tires to precise pressures before riding, yet still fits in saddlebags big and small. It holds a charge well and, crucially, works with TPU tubes, which is key for long trips where you’re more likely to need a tube to save the day.

This might be a product of where I live, but on many gravel rides, the sun is the enemy. Long dirt roads often don’t offer a ton of shade, and the Velans 2 sunglasses from Sungod have been fantastic partners. The coverage is excellent, but they still breathe well at slower speeds. I have dropped them, shoved them in pockets, and sat on them, and they have survived without a single scratch to show for it.

Gravel clothing has a bunch of definitions. For some, it’s skinsuits and aero socks. For others, it’s baggy shorts and tech tees. Yet, for most, it’s just bibs and jerseys that work well for long rides. The Gobik CX Pro jersey hits the bullseye in this regard. It is a breathable, race-cut jersey that still fits exceptionally well. Best of all, the splash of color pops against everything from desert landscapes to dark forests, helping you stay visible to the few cars driving down odd dirt roads.

While I tend to skew toward the lycra side of the gravel clothing divide, I have loved this baggy piece of cycling kit for years. These versatile and breathable pants are great for everything from a long dirty day to travel, as the ventilation and zippered pockets are just as fantastic for the airplane as they are for the bike. I have two pairs, and I find myself gravitating toward them more and more as a comfortable alternative to leg warmers or tights on colder off-road adventures.

No matter what I do, I cannot quite kick drip lube as a part of my gravel cycling. Yes, hot melt tools like the Silca Chain Waxing System are highly effective, but they don’t fully stand on their own. Even a well-waxed chain occasionally needs a refresh on a trip. Out of all the options I have tried, I have found that Faast Chain Lube does the trick best. It lasts a long time, handles grit well, and feels very smooth. It even pairs perfectly with a Silca wax base if you prefer to use a hybrid system.…

items.title: You Don’t Need Separate Bikepacking, Gravel, and Race Bikes. You Just Need the Shafer.
items.author: Alison Jaksen
items.content: The lightweight carbon Shafer (and its pedal-assist version, the Shafer HP) are designed to handle everything from gravel races to singletrack to multiday adventure
items.lbText:
The Ari Bikes Shafer HP (Photo: Ari Bikes)

Let’s be honest: if you could have infinite bikes, you probably would. Unfortunately, most of us tend to be limited by our savings accounts, our garage space, and our significant other’s desire that we spend our money on literally anything else. That’s when an elegant all-arounder like the Ari Bikes Shafer comes in.

Part race bike, part gravel rig, part long-distance hauler, the all-carbon Shafer was designed to meld high-tech performance with backcountry durability. Better yet, it actually delivers. The first jaw-dropper is the weight. The Shafer’s featherlight carbon frame clocks in at just 2 pounds—nearly a half-pound lighter than previous generations—and yet has enough clearance for 700×58c / 29×2.25-inch tires. That means riders can line up at a race one day, then slap on some fat tires and disappear into the woods the next.

Weather-sealed downtube storage, tons of frame and fork mounts, and internal dynamo routing give bikepackers and ultra-distance riders the features they need to go further. Meanwhile, dropper-post and suspension fork compatibility (up to 60 mm) means you can tackle rough trails without having to swap out for a dedicated mountain bike. Five complete build options let you further dial in the components and suspension to your specific needs, and each bike is custom-built to the rider’s measurements. Fancy, huh?

At this point, your mind might be wandering back to that crucial first point on our list of bike-accumulation obstacles: expense. While everything about Shafer—from its sleek geometry to its high-fashion paint job—screams high-performance, the hang tag isn’t what you might expect from a custom build. In fact, the Shafer’s Sport model starts at just $2,549.

That accessible price point comes courtesy of Ari Bikes’s direct-to-consumer model. Every Ari is built, tuned, and test-ridden at the brand’s Utah headquarters. Cutting out the middlemen helps the brand dramatically slash overhead without sacrificing quality. Ari also backs its bikes with a lifetime frame warranty and a 30-day love-it-or-return-it guarantee.

Now let’s say you like the sound of all that, but there’s one more category you’re looking for in your all-arounder: pedal assist. Ari Bikes has an answer to that, too. The Shafer HP , a carbon-frame gravel e-bike, is an extension of the Shafer’s ride philosophy. It combines the same geometry and versatility with a lightweight, whisper-quiet electric motor that provides a natural-feeling assist on big climbs and longer rides. Whether you’re dialing in your fitness, committing to a long daily commute, or just trying to access different types of adventures, the Shafer HP gives you all the perks of the analog bike, but with way more precise control over your effort and speed.

With a 360 Watt-hour integrated battery and an optional 160 Watt-hour range extender, the Shafer HP can handle long days between charges. Meanwhile, its 700×58c tire clearance and suspension-fork and dropper compatibility give it all the rugged adventure performance of the original Shafer. Even better news: the basic model rings in at just $4,899—a steal given its outsized capability.

Yes, it would be fun to buy three or four more bikes this season. And if you’ve been looking for an excuse to dramatically expand your fleet, we’re sorry to say the Shafer isn’t going to help you build your case. But if you’re looking for a true quiver killer that’s going to help you save money, go further, and access just about every conceivable adventure on two wheels, well, you may have just met your new ride.

Ari Bikes is a Utah-based, direct-to-consumer brand selling bikes worldwide since 2005. Ari’s mission is to help people live better now by making exceptional bikes more accessible. Backed by a 4.9-star rating, Ari offers direct-to-rider pricing, custom setup, a lifetime and transferable warranty, and a love-it-or-return-it guarantee to help deliver on that mission.

items.title: The U.S. Has a New UCI Gravel Race, and It Is a Stunner
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: Borderlands Gravel in Arizona joins BWR Utah and Highlands Gravel on the UCI Gravel World Series in 2027
items.lbText:
In 2027, the US will have two new UCI gravel races, with Borderlands Gravel the latest to join the UCI’s selection of sanctioned gravel races. The race in Douglas, Arizona, runs along the far southeastern border of Arizona and Mexico, with a short stint in New Mexico along the way.

The 2026 edition took place on November 14th, and Velo was on-site to get a sense of the unique event that melds the area’s American and Mexican identities.

Next year, the race will use the same terrain, but with more at stake as it will be one of three UCI Gravel World Series stops in the United States. BWR Utah in Cedar City will be the other new addition to the UCI calendar, while Highlands Gravel returns for another year.

The course, which will be an early qualifier for the 2028 UCI Gravel World Championship, will be an 87-mile largely out-and-back course with 5,000 feet of climbing. Half of the route runs directly along sections of the border wall, with the race using the gravel service road that cuts through high desert vistas, washes, and creosote fields.

The second half of the out-and-back leaves the border behind and climbs its way up one of the “sky islands” of Arizona. The climbing is gradual at first, with 14 miles at 2%, before a 1.6-mile, 8% wall that crests just shy of 6,000 feet of altitude.

The elements will only add to the challenge of the day. This year, it was mud and wind that challenged the riders, with rare November rains soaking the course. In other years, heat and sand could play a factor.

The constant factor? The gravel road that cuts through the Coronado National Forest in the New Mexico portion of the out-and-back is some of the most spectacular gravel riding I have encountered this year.

From a racing perspective, Borderlands Gravel will continue to be one of the last gravel races of the year, and thus one of the first opportunities to qualify for the next UCI Gravel World Championship in AlUla, Saudi Arabia, giving riders nearly a year to prepare for the event.

items.title: Time for Tour de France Hommes? Marlen Reusser Thinks So
items.author: ahood
items.content: 'I don’t want to be a decoration of a male sport': Marlen Reusser explains why the men's Tour de France needs to add 'Hommes' to its name.
items.lbText:
Marlen Reusser says it's time to call the men's race the Tour de France Hommes. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Marlen Reusser says it’s time for cycling to rethink how it brands races by gender.

Instead of having the Tour de France and the Tour de France Femmes , the Swiss star suggests adding “Hommes” to the men’s race, all in the name of fairness.

Speaking on the Domestique Hotseat podcast, the Movistar rider said her frustration peaked at October’s presentation of the 2027 routes in Paris, where Tour director Christian Prudhomme and Tour de France Femmes director Marion Rousse shared the stage.

“The Tour director comes on the stage and introduces the women’s Tour director, Marion Rousse, at his side. You feel like he’s ruling it all, that it’s his Tour, the men’s Tour, and we are guests there,” Reusser told Domestique . “Marion is also allowed to say something, to say hello, but we’re the guests.”

Reusser first raised the subject with Cycling Weekly in October, first saying she thinks “Hommes” should be part of the conversation.

Prudhomme has said the Tour de France is the traditional name for the men’s race, which dates to 1903.

Speaking to Cycling Weekly after last month’s route presentation, he said that “the Tour is the Tour, and we’re absolutely delighted that there’s another race.”

In French, “femmes” translates to women, and “hommes” is men.

Reusser was quick to credit organizers for the growth of the women’s race since its launch in its current form in 2022.

But she also wants that progress to extend to the language surrounding cycling’s races.

“But I wish that very soon it’s not the Tour, it’s the men’s Tour. And we are guests that can have a little Tour also, but it’s the Tour,” she said. “And you can check the dates, from this to this is the women’s, from this to this is the men’s.

“And it doesn’t matter, and it can be just as interesting, just as cool,” she said. “I don’t want to be a decoration of a male sport.”

The issue is becoming a talking point as more races and teams have both men’s and women’s events and squads.

Many of the major teams, like Lidl-Trek and Movistar, do not differentiate between the two genders.

Some races that have both men’s and women’s editions follow the pattern used by ASO. Other examples are the Giro d’Italia and Giro d’Italia Women or the Vuelta a España and La Vuelta Femenina.

Reusser told Domestique that tradition shouldn’t prevent change.

“Let’s say the UCI decided there is a rule that you cannot put ‘women’ or ‘femmes’ in the name of a race when you don’t have the same in the name of the men’s race. Then you could not say it’s tradition,” she said. “You would just have to change it, and I think it would go fast. It’s a matter of how much people really want to change stuff.”

Right now, there are no official UCI rules outlining how race organizers name their events.

Reusser — who cited her background in medicine — said words help establish the hierarchy.

“If we word things as standard men, we think standard men,” she said. “So if we want to have it different, we need to start wording things different.”
